speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to lay on the table a copy of the notice sent to all the officers of the Department of Public Works charged with the purchase of materials and supplies and the certifying of accounts for the same, under the different branches of the chief architect, the chief engineer and the superintendent of telegraphs. One of these notices was sent to the chief engineer's staff on September 16, 1908, one to the chief architect's staff on December 18, and one to the superintendent of telegraphs' stall on December 18. As the notices are all in the same language, I need read only one:
Sir,-I am directed by the hon. the Minister of Public Works to call your attention in a special manner to the question of purchase



of materials and supplies required for the use of the Department of Public Works, and which are obtained either by yourself personally or under your supervision, and to impress upon you the necessity of exercising the greatest care and caution in obtaining same at the very best possible prices, and that the most careful scrutiny should be given to all accounts before certification.
I am also to caution you emphatically regarding the acceptance of any gifts or favours of any kind at the hands of contractors or merchants with whom you may have dealings on behalf of the department and, further, if any such transaction should come to your knowledge, that it is your duty as an official of the department to report same at once to the minister or deputy minister, in order that such investigation may be made and action taken as may be deemed proper.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
Secretary.

This includes $325,000, pay of the force, and $425,000 for subsistence. There is an increase of $25,000 for pay and a decrease of $25,000 for subsistence, leaving the appropriation the same as last year. This estimate is for a force of 700 men, 500 being in Alberta and Saskatchewan, 100 in the Yukon, and 100 in the Northwest Territories. We estimate that the cost per man in Alberta and Saskatchewan will be $900 per year and in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon $1,500 per year. The increase of $25,000 in the pay is due to the rapid settlement of the provinces, which affords so much employment for labour generally that it is difficult to get men to join the force. The pay is 50 cents per man per day with an increase of 5 cents each year to the maximum of one dollar per day. But if there is a disinclination on the part of the younger men to enlist, it has been found that there is, especially among the non-commissioned officers a disposition to re-enlist at the expiration of their term of five years. We have therefore a good many veterans in the force, so that the pay, which commences at 60 cents and goes to a maximum of $1 per day, is on the average 85 cents.
What is the disposition of the 500 men in the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

We have in the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan 500 men, 100 in the Yukon and 100 in the Territory. We have 12 principal stations distributed in Alberta, Saskatchewan, the Territory and the Yukon. _ In each of these 12 stations is a district, at the head of which is an officer and a small staff, and each one of these stations has a certain number of detached stations. We have 150 subsidiary stations dependent upon these 12. In Alberta there are 63 such stations; in Saskatchewan, 70; in the Yukon, 10; in the Northwest Territories, 7. We propose to distribute them from the United States boundary line up to Whitehorse and Dgwson in the Yukon, to the mouth of the Mackenzie river in the north and to the Hudson bay in the east.
How many men have you in Alberta?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Two hundred and fifty, and 250 in Saskatchewan, 100 in the Northwest Territories, and 100 in the Yukon. There are 12 posts where the men are distributed. My non. friend is familiar with the duties of those men. They include not only the duties of police officers in the ordinary sense, but they are of great assistance to colonization and settlement. I may say that the force is all the time patrolling; the men are all the time on horseback, visiting every settlement and every settler, visiting the ranchmen, asking if there are any complaints, rectifying erroneous reports, and reporting anything out of the ordinary. I may say that though we ask for an appropriation of $750,000, the cost to the federal treasury is only $600,000, because we receive $75,000 each from the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
What rifles is the force anned with now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Lee-Met-ford and the Winchester.

I would like a little more explanation as to the disposition of the men. Is it a part of the policy of the department gradually to withdraw the men from the more thickly settled portions of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the large towns for instance, the large villages along the line of railway, and distribute them to the outlying portions, where there is lesser civic authority, and influences that come from the more settled conditions, especially in view of the fact that the time is approaching when these provinces must, the same as British Columbia and Manitoba, look after their own civic affairs, in so far as this force takes the place of bailiffs and constables, and that kind of officer which, in other provinces, is provided by the provincial authority. So it is a matter of some importance to know whether the policy of the department is to withdraw from the older portions and gradually to distribute the force, send them into the outlying districts where the power of the civil authority is not so strong. There is another point which I would like to mention to the Prime Minister, and I will be frank about it: Does he allow local party interests to have any part or lot in this matter, or is he keeping this force in that respect on the high level of a military force? Is he sure that it is not used in any way to advance the interest of-we may be frank about it-the party, or the party representatives?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With regard to the first point, my hon. friend has anticipated tne policy of the department; it is gradually to withdraw police protection from the larger and older sections of the community and give it to the new settlements. I am afraid that for some years to come we will be forced to keep a portion of the force on the frontier of the United States until settlement becomes thicker there. It is a matter of necessity for the protection of the revenue, and of the settler, and the preservation of peace, to keep a little closer watch on the line than in the interior. But gradually we are reducing the force in the larger towns, and extending it northward to the newer settlements. The day cannot be far distant when the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan can dispense with a large portion of the force; but I imagine that as long as immigration flows in at the rate it is doing now, it would be a mistake to withdraw the force altogether. The sight of the uniform is an encouragement to the settler, he feels more secure; especially those who come from the continent of Europe feel more safe when they know that the police constable is not far distant, and they can have recourse to

him, not only for the purpose of protection against violence, but for all sorts of needs. If the settler feels a difficulty about anything he goes to the police force, and that force is of great value to him in many ways. With regard to the second question of my hon. friend, I do not think that my hon. friend has received any complaint of the action of the police, I think it has been kept absolutely free from any partisan action. I have received complaints, perhaps on one or two occasions. The instructions are very severe to the officers that they should not interfere in politics in any way. But more than one or two complaints I have not received, and I do not think my hon. friend has received any either, or at most, very few.
The right hon. gentleman says there are a hundred men in the Yukon. Would he tell me how they are distributed in the Yukon?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have reduced the force there from 300 to 100. At present there are two chief stations in the Yukon, at Dawson and at Whitehorse. In the Dawson division there are substations at Town Station, Grand Forks, Selkirk, Quartz creek, Granville, Selkirk and Forty Miles. In the Whitehorse division there are substations at Carcross, Livingstone creek and Champagne's Landing. They are looking after the miners chiefly. Of course it is our intention to reduce the force and eventually to withdrraw it completely. The experiment was tried two years ago in Dawson of having their own police force, but it did not work and they had to fall back upon the Mounted Police.

As far as I am concerned, I agree entirely with the general idea of the Prime Minister that the force is of inestimable value to us and to the Northwest. The only points I think we ought to guard against, beside those I have mentioned, are that we do not give up its consummation, in the not very far distant future, of the idea that the provinces as they grow become densely populated and get their municipalities organized will ultimately have to look after their own police work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

There are two influences which, T suppose, the Prime Minister has constantly upon him. The local governments themselves, for various reasons, would be loath to see a single man of the Mounted Police disappear from either of the provinces and the localities seem to have a decided preference for the Mounted Police over a provincial constable or officer. These two influences would work towards the perpetuation of the force in all its fulness and it is against that that I think the Prime Minister is wise in having his policy defin-Sir WTLFRTD LAURTFR.
itely stated and currently carried out. The real need comes where settlement is more sparse. But, I think, that no one can question for a single moment that the force has been worth its cost a hundred times over in the development of the Northwest. It has not only been a credit to Canada but it has really been the backbone and support of the people of that country. It has kept order, maintained respect for the law and it has given to scattered families and homesteaders a real peace and comfort to know that the mounted policeman was within hail and made his occasional visit. Nothing could compensate for the loss of that, and I think the Dominon has done properly and rightly in keeping this force at its high level and distributing it through those portions of the Northwest. It is one thing, that, if it is kept out of party politics and kept up to its original excellence, there will never be much quarrel between the two sides of the House upon it.
The right hon. Prime Minister did not know what the force in the Yukon cost. There are a hundred men, I understand?

We have several times asked the question whether the government did not think, in view of the reducing population of the Yukon, that they could do with less men and less expense. It seems a pretty large item for policing that territory. if the population is about 10,000, it costs $10.50 a head for policing that country. When the police force was first sent there the population was very much larger
than it is now and things were supposed to be not in as high a state of civilization as at the present time. Do the government think it necessary to keep up such a large force (100) to look after about 10,000 people, and do they think that the expense cannot be reduced materially in a part of the country where we are told that the streets of Dawson are just as quiet as the streets of Ottawa, and where there is no more lawlessness and no more disposition to lawlessness than in the older settled portions of the country? If that is a fact it seems to me that we should be able to make some reduction in the number of the force and in the expense that is incurred in maintaining it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it is quite true, and it is our boast that the streets of Dawson, Whitehorse and all the creeks in the Yukon are just as safe as are the streets of the city of Ottawa, but that is the result, I believe, of the presence of the police. If the police were not there I think the result would be very different and we could not hope that the streets of those placesovould be as secure as they are to-day. There are now 10,000 people in the Yukon, but it is a mining camp. Mining camps are not proverbially very orderly, and unless we have police the order may not be what it is today. At all events, that is our supposition and that is the representation which is made to us. We started in the Yukon with 300 men and we have reduced the force to 100 men. It is our intention to reduce it still further as we think we are justified in doing so. At the present time I do not know whether it would be justified or not. We have had no mail from the Yukon of late and we would not undertake to reduce the force unless we had had previous communication with the commissioner, Mr. Henderson. If we are advised that we can, with security to the territory, reduce the force ii is our intention to do so. At the same time I would remind my hon. friend that I would doubt the wisdom of withdrawing the whole force at the present time. The Yukon is far away from communication. At one time we had information that there was a party of desperadoes in Skagway that wanted to raid the territory and that was the first reason that induced us to send in the force. If that was the case, and I think there was good reason for so believing^ for self-protection it is advisable that we should not withdraw the force altogether at this moment but that we should reduce it as far as circumstances will allow.

While we may not take the force away entirely it does seem to me that it might be materially reduced without any great danger of a disturbance of the" peace. The minister says that mining camps are proverbially turbu-

lent. We have two important mining camps in Ontario, Cobalt and Gowganda. The provincial constables look after the policing of those mining camps, and we do not hear of any outrages being committed there any more than in the Yukon. Yet there is not one constable there for every ten, perhaps every fifteen, that there is in the Yukon. With the reduced population, and with the turbulent element largely gone, if we can believe the information which we have received from year to year, it does seem to me that it ought to be part of the duty and of the desire of the government to get an annual report from their inspectors on that phase of the question. There is in the Yukon a quasi form of government that ought to do a great deal in the administration of justice to relieve us of the necessity of maintaining a police force there. It is true, we have reduced the force from 300 to 100, but still it seems to me that the 100 is a large number of men to look after 10,000 people, if there are that number-because we are sometimes told that there are only
5,000	or 6,000 in that country. Does the force d,o any other material work that could not be done by civil officials? They used to collect the customs revenues, I think; are they doing that work any more than they did, or are they simply performing the duties of police constables?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will agree with me that there is no comparison whatever between the Yukon and Gowganda and Cobalt. The latter places are within easy reach of the forces of the government of Ontario in case a riot should break out. But if we had a riot at Dawson, unless we had a military force there, how could we assert the authority of the law? This consideration alone is, I think, sufficient to warrant us in maintaining the force there. We do not want to see a repetition there of the early days of California, when every man was his own constable. We must maintain law and order in the Yukon. I agree with my hon. friend that we should reduce the force when possible, and we are reducing it gradually. My hon. friend asks if the force continues to do the service it did at one time in collecting the revenue. We are gradually withdrawing it from that duty, and when we do that altogether, there will be less occasion for the number of men we have. I think we have reduced the force as rapidly as it has been possible to do it without jeopardizing the peace of the country.
Are there any of the police force in Manitoba now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, not at all.
There is none in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
Is there any in the unorganized territories?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. In all the Northwest Territories, including the Yukon, we have 150 stations and 700 men.

Of all the great changes which have taken place in our great west, the one which causes the old timers the greatest regret is the passing away of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. For some time the withdrawal of the police from the centres has been going on, and we do not see them on our streets to-day as we did in former years. I personally endorse the policy the right hon. gentleman has followed, but I am sorry that we cannot see more of these men. They have done a great and valuable service in our country; they have served the country and served it well, and I am sorry that we cannot do more for these men than we have done. I am quite in accord with all the right hon. gentleman has done, and I support the vote.

I wish to point out a reason why the vote should be taken at the figure stated, even though later experience should show that the number of men mentioned in the vote is not required. In a country like the Yukon it is a very difficult thing to estimate a year beforehand what number of police may be required. At any time there may be a fresh discovery and an influx from the neighbouring portions of Alaska or from other places, of a population which would necessitate the presence of a large force of the police. I think in any case that when we are making an appropriation of this kind we should provide for a sufficient number of men to render the force capable of coping with any possible contingency that may arise.

I supposed that hon. gentlemen would look at it. The reason for the large increase under civil government is that whereas formerly we had only 36 employees in the permanent inside service there were in the neighbourhood of 200 in the service in Ottawa who were paid from the outside service vote. The department was organized first when Sir Hector Langevin was minister and further under Mr. Hyman. Now under the provisions of the Civil Service Act instead of there being 36 in the inside service there will in future be 237. That accounts for the increase in this vote. If my hon. friend will turn to other items he will find there is a reduction corresponding to the increase under civil government.
Is the reduction in one case equal to the increase in the other?
Yea, with the exception of some increases in salaries and in the staff.
How much additional cost is incurred; by the transition of these 237 officials into the inside service?

The memorandum I have is that the present salaries amount to $237,387 to be increased to $263,175, or an increase of $25,787 under the new organization. Then there is one additional clerk in the third division sub-division A provided for. Then there are the statutory increases for 1909-10 to 196 employees, $5,262.52. Then we make provision for additional appointments or any other changes necessary in the departmental staff, $5,000. The balance, covering the difference between the annual increases in salaries authorized by
the orders in council of 1908, and the portion of such annual increases actually paid to employees to be transferred to civil government during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1909, $8,958.81.
Would not that be part of the statutory increases already provided?

No, they were special increases by orders in council, and these are set forth in the orders in council which have been laid on the table. That makes a total of $25,728.98. In the memorandum from the Finance Department, on page 26, that amount is given just as I have given it here, as a footnote. The other increases are accounted for by the increases to those who were already members of the permanent staff. We have picked out all those who were in the inside temporary service and who have been brought, by virtue of the Civil Service Act, into the permanent staff, and we deduct their salaries from what had been hitherto provided for in these miscellaneous votes, and add them under the head of civil government.

Where the civil servants have received an additional amount over what they were receiving heretofore, for the purpose of putting them in a certain class under the new Act, do they receive this year the statutory increase?
They begin to earn their statutory increase, but do not get it until they have served a year.
Did they get it last year?
Those who were in the outside service did not receive statutory increases. Their increases had to be by order in council.
What has been done with that class who were induced to resign and go into the outside service for the purpose of getting in in a higher class at an increased salary?
There was not one instance of that kind in my department.
I am credibly informed there were some in the other departments.
I can only answer for my own.

The other night this point was raised. Take the order in council of May 5, 1908, which is in these words: ' That authority be granted for the continued employment of the undermentioned officers in one of the permanent branches of the Department of Public Works at the salaries hereinafter specified from July 1, 1908, to July 1, 1909.' The order in council is silent as to whether the salary set opposite the name of each one was the salary of the preceding year. As far as we can judge
3GC7

from anything said in the order in council, each one may have had $150 or $500 added to his salary. Were these the same salaries that these employees were being paid the preceding year?

In quite a number of cases there were slight increases in salary provided for by that order in council. Every year there must have been an order in council, for the continuance of those engaged in the outside staff. The appointments were for the year and were renewed by order in council and the salaries provided for.

It seems to me the order in council ought to state what is really being done or else council may be very easily misled. Of course the minister might have gone over it in detail with his colleagues and shown exactly what he did.
That information is given to the Treasury Board and that board has before it the salaries of the previous year in every case.

But the Treasury Board gets what comes before it second-hand. It is a subsidiary council of the council. Surely the minister does not reserve the question of increases for the Treasury Board alone? The increases in salary come first before council. If they go to the Treasury Board first, the report from that board must come back before the council. It is not the Treasury Board which can either give salaries or increase them; it is the council alone which can do that. The Treasury Board has other duties to perform; they have to see that the regulations and conditions are the proper ones as prescribed by law. That opens the whole question. The minister will remember that I stated in that general debate that in the orders in council which had been brought down later, a large number of these outside employees received special increases running from $50 up to $200 or $300, and I tried to calculate the total increase which had been, as I contended, given by the minister outside the spirit of the Act, to take effect on the 1st of September, as grading these into the service under the new Civil Service Act. The whole of it was not shown, unless we can find out what increases were given by this order in council, which purports, on the face of it, to provide simply for a continuance of office, and impliedly a continuance of salary. Now, the minister says that while it was a continuance in office it was in many cases an increase of salary. I do not want to take up too much time to find out just what increases were given, but in that large number of clerks, the minister will see there is room for a good deal to happen under that concealed order. It is rather blind, I think, to say the least of it. The minister is sending down an order in coun-Mr. FOSTER.
cil with reference to employees that have been employed year after year, and asking that they be continued at the salaries placed opposite their names. I think the inference is that the salaries are simply continued salaries.

The usual course was followed in this case. The order in council of the previous year would show the salaries which were paid in that year, and, as is customary, and as I think my hon. friend will agree is a proper course in this case, this recommendation to council was referred to the Treasury Board. The Treasury Board then had before it the salaries of each of these officers had received the previous year, and saw what were the recommendations for increases; the Treasury Board then reported to council, and upon the report and recommendation of the Treasury Board the order was passed. I do not think my hon. friend is right in calling it a concealed order.
Well, it is a blind order.

Not at all. The most my hon. friend can say is that it does not show what were the salaries these officers received in the previous year. Though I would be sorry to see the item delayed. I will be glad to lay on the table of the House a copy of the order in council of the previous year so that my hon. friend can compare the two.

That raises the question as to whether this was the custom in the other departments. We have found out so far in our investigation that some of the ministers in some of the departments carried out this whole business on a different plane from others, and it raises the question now as to whether the ministers generally, in reporting to council with reference to the vast outside body, gave increases then, upon which afterwards special increases, sometimes repeated, have been made. In the other* case we saw what the special increases were; they could not be put in any other way but in the first continuing order. If all the reports had been the same as my hon. friend's, we do not know, by looking at it, how much the increase was given and in what cases. I would like to go into the new system and ascertain how each division of the service entered it; and if the minister will amend that report that he brought down with his order in council of the 5th May, 1908, by having one of his clerks put alongside the list that is here each case of increase, probably they were not all increases, that would lighten the labour somewhat. If he would do that, and have it ready before we get into the Civil Service discussion, I would be very glad.
I will do that.

Then I raised the question before by what authority it was that you come in along the last of August, and you make increases, and you date the increase back by the order in council, two months, may be, to the beginning of the then fiscal year. I cannot find any authority in the Civil Service for that. I do find that this has been done, that you come down to parliament and you ask that an increase be granted, and that the increase be voted to take effect at a certain time. But out of the vote that you can, on the 27th day of August, make an increase of salary of $100 or $200 to men in the service, and then say that it may be dated back to the 1st of April-I do not find any authority for that. Anyway, it seems to be a rather dangerous form of proceeding, you are doing what parliament has had no advisement of. That is altogether different from the case where you come down in an estimate and say: Here, I want $50, or $100, or $200 increase in this item for such a clerk, and I want to pay him from the first of the year, or from any particular month.

I do not know whether that could be done in the case of one who was under the Civil Service Act, but I presume it could not be done. I would agree with my hon. friend in that respect. But with respect to those who are on the temporary, and what is known as the outside service, that authority has always been recognized, because the vote is for a lump sum, and when the question came up with regard to fixing the date from which the increase would tal^e effect, my deputy informed me that it had been the practice ever since he had been in the department, and there seems to be no limitation under the Act with regard to that power. It occurred in two or three cases, I think that was done by the order of May. My hon. friend is aware that the order in council was not an order made under the old Civil Service Act, it was made before, the new Act came into force-that was my information. The vote being a general one and these officers not being under the old Civil Service Act, the council, if they thought fit to do so, could fix a date anterior to the order irom which the increase of salary would take effect. Now, with regard to making the increases themselves, I think we threshed that out pretty fully some time ago. But I think my hon. friend will realize that as there were a large number of officials who were going to be brought by force of law under the Civil Service Act and were to be placed side by side with those who were under the new Act, it was proper that the deputy minister of my department should have regard to the merits, so far as possible, of the different officers, to their length of service, the importance of the duties which thev were discharging, and endeavour to do justice as between them all, and so start
them upon the 1st of September upon a proper and justifiable basis, leaving their remuneration and their classification after that to be fixed from time to time under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. That is what he sought to do, and it is what I sought to assist him in doing so far as my knowledge would enable me.

I do not wish to go again over the discussion we had the other night, but I would point out to the minister that I do not think his ground is a good ground. He may say that he thought he had more liberty under the outside vote than he had under the appropriation for what we call the regular Civil Service. But in theory they are the same. You ask for your vote to pay for the services of your officers, and, when you get your vote you administer the fund under the authority given. The fact that these men were to be brought in on September 1, and up to that time had not been brought in, does not, I think, make against the argument that the spirit of the legislation of last year was to place the service on a permanent basis and on a basis of competition and merit in appointments, which, up to that time, had not been the case. As I said then, so I believe now, that the outside service should have been administered in the spirit of that Act. While I do not want to go over that discussion again, I find that there are new appointments, for which, as yet, I think we have no reasons. A draughtsman was appointed in the chief engineer's branch at $700, the appointment being made by order in council on August 6, 1908, and dated back to April 1, 1908.
That was the beginning of the fiscal year.

But the appointment was not made at the beginning of the fiscal year, but was dated back. Now, the Civil Service Act provides, both with reference to the outside and the inside service, that no appointment shall be made until the office has been created, in the case of the regular Civil Service, and, in any case, until the amount has been voted by parliament. The whole spirit of the Act is against dating appointments back. Mr. F. O. Hamel was appointed at $700 in the chief architect's branch. What is the explanation of that appointment?
Mr. Hamel is a draughtsman, and the services of a draughtsman were required and accordingly he was appointed. That is all I can say.

That answer might be set up and stereotyped. Was the appointment so urgent that it could not be left over from August 6, when it was made, to September 1, when the machinery of the

Civil Service Act would be at the disposal of the minister for all appointments?

There was a good deal of work on hand last year, and the chief architect was very much in need of additional assistance. I was very desirous, as far as possible, to carry out the views expressed in the House that architectural work should be done in the department. So, it became absolutely essential to have additional help.
The minister has not been very explicit as to what would have happened had he waited for twenty-five days later and made the appointment in the regular form.

Plans on important public works would have been delayed. This young man had been employed temporarily because the services of one of his profession were needed, so he was actually in the office before the order in council was passed, and I think probably had been workins from about April 1.
I suppose he must have been there, or the minister, surely, would not have paid him.
There was an item relating to rents that stood over. Is it to come up this afternoon?
I tried to bring it forward two or three times before. I shall be glad to have it dealt with this afternoon.
The hon. minister promised us some information on the subject. I do not wish the item to stand any longer than is necessary.
There is a new appointment at $1,250, the appointee being Mr. Arthur Barsalou-made on the same date, 6th August. Apparently, the minister could not wait twenty-five days in this case either.
Unfortunately, his predecessor died unexpectedly, and we had to fill the office. Mr. Barsalou's salary was not dated back, was it ?
Yes, to April 1. The minister could not have had both the living and the dead on the salary list at the same time.
My deputy tells me that Mr. Barsalou was in the department before that, perhaps performing the duties while his predecessor was ill.
Then, he was not appointed before the death of his predecessor ?

He was appointed because of his predecessor's death, but I fancy he was discharging the duties during his predecessor's illness.
_ Mr. FOSTER. The minister will get the information to which I have referred ?

Yes.
Contingencies, $15,000.
Does this cover printing and stationery ?
Yes. It is the same a3 last year.

I believe - this covers the printing of the annual report of the Public Works Department. I desire to mention a matter which was called to my attention by a chemistry professor and a prominent paper manufacturer in Montreal recently. These gentlemen tell me that the report of the Public Works Department and other blue-books are printed upon paper which will not stand the test of time. Are steps taken to have a limited number of these reports printed upon paper of such a character that these books will be available twenty-five or fifty years from now ?

I have not heard that question raised before. It concerns the Stationery Department rather than my own. I shall be glad to bring the matter to the attention of that department to see if there is anything in the point my hon. friend raises.

The point is this:	If the
paper on which the records of the Public Works Department and others are printed is of wood pulp or chemical pulp, in twenty-five or thirty years from now it will crumble away and the books made of it will be useless. I would ask the minister if he will have inquiries made whether the paper used is wood pulp or chemical pulp paper. If it is, it would be well that a limited number of copies of reports should be printed on better paper.
I suppose my hon. friend would not suggest parchment
No, but linen paper.
I su-ppose there is a difference between ground pulp paper and chemical ?
The reports of the different departments are found in the bound sessional records. Whether that is the same kind of paper or not, I do not know.

I think the bound sessional Tecords are simply the regular blue books. However, the matter is worth looking into, because these records should be preserved.
Rents, repairs, furniture, heating, &c.-Dominion buildings-rents, &c., $200,000.

Our time is somewhat limited. We shall probably not have much leisure left this week, and next week will be a busy one, according to the work arranged for. I understood the Minister of Finance was anxious to get a supply bill of the supplementary estimates and such

others as were neecssary. While we are willing to facilitate that, 'we do not propose to shove through all these items within the time proposed. So, I think, if the ministers want to get their original estimates through, they should give their time to the urgent portions of them.
We might take some of the items under 'Public Works-Miscellaneous.' This includes salaries for a number of employees.
But they are salaries for next year.
Yes, but standing in the same position as those under 'Civil Government' that we have just put through. And the money is needed.
This is a very inclusive item. I think you will see a lot of discussion on it.
It relates altogether to my own department.

But you have here the Deep Waterways Commission and other important items. Of course, the minister can take up time on this if he likes. But my desire is to facilitate what seems to be a matter of some urgency. There are some Votes in Civil Government left.
Civil Government-Department of Mines- salaries, $148,831.50.

With reference to this department, I have been nuzzled over it. It is difficult for me to find out how it came, and pretty nearly as difficult to find out ' whither it goeth.' The minister, it may be, will enlighten me. Under the Department of Mines, he has fifty of the old permanents, and thirty-eight whom he has taken in from outside. Where did he get the fifty permanents? What does the department in that respect include? Does it take in the whole of what was the old Geological Survey?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The permanent officials, according to my addition, number 46 not 50. However, these are the permanent members of the old Geological Survey, and also several permanent officers of the Mines Branch of , the Department of the Interior. The Mines Department, as at present constituted, is made up of these two-the Geological Survey and the Mines Branch of the Department of the Interior, over which Dr. Haanel presided. I think I have not increased the number of officials-not very considerably at all events. That is whence the department came ; as to ' whither it goeth,' that remains to be seen It is going along very successfully, and doing, I think, very good work.

There are three permanents, a deputy minister, one in subdivision B of the 1st division, and one in the third division, subdivision A. Where did these three come from ? I suppose the deputy minister was Mr. Low, director of the Geological Survey.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes. When the department was organized, he occupied the position of director and deputy head of the Geological Survey and became deputy minister of the Department of Mines. Mr. Marshall was accountant of the Geological Survey and is now accountant of the Mines Department.
At the same salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes. His salary was $2,275. We are giving him an increase of $100.
That is the statutory increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
Then, there is a third division clerk, sub-division 'A'. Who is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is Miss B. Urquhart, stenographer and she was in the geological survey.
Last year this clerk received $837.50 and the estimate this year is $937.50. How is it that she comes in with an increase of salary instead of being transferred at the same salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am advised that this lady was a junior second-class clerk and the Act provided that she would go into a class with a minimum salary of $900.
- Mr. FOSTER. Do the junior second-class clerks go into that division or into the $800 minimum division?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Into 'A' of the third
division. She goes into the class from $900 to $1,200.

Well then $37.50 would be the statutory increase for her. Whether this is the place or not to raise the question, it comes in here. What is the basis, supposing they are getting $700, or whatever they are getting as junior second-class clerks, upon which you put these into the $900 to $1,200 division instead of the $800 to $1,600 division?

That would depend entirely on the quality of the work that the clerk was doing. It is open to the minister to decide into which of these divisions the clerk would go. Wherever the salary was common to two divisions certain clerks, if they got so much salary, say $800, who were doing work that is of a quality that is intended for the third division would go

into that- division, whereas, certain other clerks, who were getting $800 and who were doing work of a quality which is intended for the second division, would be put into ' B ' of the second division instead of 'A' of the third division.
Is that left entirely for the minister to say?

As far as those in the service, before 1st September, are concerned, the commissioners have nothing to do with it. In future it will depend upon examination. In future, applicants for entry into the service will go into ' B ' of the third division or ' B ' of the second division, according to the examination they pass.

But where there is a certain salary, such as that which has been mentioned, the discretion is entirely with the minister as to whether they shall go into the $800 to $1,600 division or the $900 to $1,200 division?
If they were in the service, yes. In future that cannot occur.

Then there are five from the outside service in the first division. Was there any addition made to the salary of these five during the six months preceding the first of September, or during any part of the fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not think there were any increases made. I am advised by the director that there were no increases made to bring any of these officials into other classes than those that the salaries which they were then receiving entitled them to.

There are 38 brought in from the outside service and, as I understand, the minister says there were no increases in the salaries of the 38 immediately prior to the 31st September and that they were transferred on the same salaries as those which they were receiving during the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Quite right.

So that in this case there was no boosting of salaries in order to give them a better position. Well, I commend the minister for the policy of his department. It is in strong contrast with the policy of some of the other departments, the head of one of which is sitting very close to us now.

Would the minister be good enough to give a general idea of what the extra clerks are doing? The Mines branch has only been organized two or three years but the increase in the number of clerks in the geological survey and the Mr. FISHER.
mines branch has been considerable. What is the cause of the increase and what is the great need of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is news to me to be told that there has been a considerable increase in the number of technical officers or clerks of any kind in the Department of Mines.
Would the minister give us the expenditure five years ago and the expenditure to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have not the expenditure five years ago. The expenditure has increased somewhat in the last few years, but it has not increased very largely. The additions to the staff, speaking from recollection, have been those of technical officers. We have in the Mines Branch, several new technical men, mining engineers and others of that kind. But as to clerks, stenographers and other officials of that kind, there has been very little increase in the department. I am not speaking from notes or memoranda but I know the demands made upon me to increase the staff have not been met very largely because we could not find the men we desired to have in those positions.
What was the expenditure in the mines branch and the geological survey branch during the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The total vote for 1908-9 was, for the Mines branch, $100,000. This year the vote is $81,000. For the assay office in Vancouver the vote last year was $26,000 and this year it is $18,000, a decrease in both cases. There is an increase, which will probably equal the amount of that decrease, in the geological survey vote from $204,750 to $240,000. Therefore, I think, we are hardly open to criticism for having increased the expenditure.

I am very glad to see that the minister is so well satisfied with the amount of work being done for that amount of money. If we will look back ten years we will see that the department got along with about $110,000. When the expenditure was increased from that to over $200,000, we would naturally expect that there would be some material benefits derived from it. Is the minister continuing the practice of allowing officers of the survey to work for private companies during the summer months and then to come back in the fall and step into the department, their salaries going on as usual ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I would prefer that the discussion on the work of the department should be on the main estimates when I shall have considerable information to give. The work that is being done today bv the department in infinitely greater than it was ten years ago; whether it be

greater relatively to the increased expenditure I cannot for the moment say. The policy of the department is not to permit its officers to do private work. There have been one or two instances in which the officers of the department were needed by explorers, private companies if you will, for a season's work. They could not find experienced men along these special lines elsewhere in Canada and in one or two instances, only one instance this last year, an officer was permitted to leave the department, but without salary, and to return afterwards, giving to the department all the inforamtion he had obtained while working for the private company.
He was of course well paid by the private company?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have no doubt he was probably paid more than he would be paid by the government, and right there you touch on a very important point. Our difficulty is to retain in the service of the government the best men. During the last few years two or three officers of the survey have left our employment simply because instead of being satisfied with $2,000 a year or so they have been able to receive $5,000 from private companies. In one or two cases the question for us was whether we should permit one of our best men to take service with a company exploring for coal for a few months, or lose his services altogether as his resignation was practically in our hands. If it were a general practice it perhaps might not be a good one. Of course while that officer is in the employ of the private company he is not paid by the government. There a few private geologists throughout the country, and many mining engineers, but we have in the survey most of the prominent geologists in Canada, and I believe it is desirable to occasionally permit them to leave the employment of the government in the summer months and do work for a private company', they giving to the government for publication in the reports the information they had obtained. There is another practice of the department somewhat similar. At present there is very great interest in the exploration of iron ore deposits throughout Canada, and within the last two or three weeks three applications have been made to me to permit one of the officers who is an expert in iron and the magno-metric survey of iron deposits to make surveys of privately owned property. Some of these applications have come from within a short distance of Ottawa. We permit the officers to do the work, and I think it is conducive to the development of the iron industry. It does not cost the government very much, we simply loan the man for a few weeks. We are not interfering with the business of any outside geologists or mining engineers because there is a great dearth of specialists in Canada for this work.

The minister has laid down a very dangerous proposition. He knows well that for five years one of the prominent men of the geological survey, in company with a number of employees of the government, located the best coal mines in the Northwest, and hardly had he handed over his report to the department, and before it could be circulated amongst the public generally, he went into the employment of a private company and started out west and located twenty-six of the best coal mines in that territory. A $6,000,000 company, controlled by a few men who are able to get this official away from the department, has been organized. If the minister will go back a few years he will see that other men have been doing the same thing, going out for members of parliament who were interested in these mines, spending their summers on the work and then stepping in to the department and getting their salaries during the winter months when they had nothing else to do. True, they may turn over the information to the government but it is after the companies have made all the use they could make of it. It is a very dangerous precedent for the minister to lay down.

The remarks of the member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) are worthy of considerable attention. It "is a vicious principle to lay down, that these men who are presumably acting for the country at large and who acquire experience in the discharge of their duties, should place their knowledge at the disposal of private persons or companies. To let these men go out and give the benefit of their information to private corporations for a few months in the year and then come back and spend the winter in the government service, dumped again on the people at a good salary, and go out again the next spring or summer to the private corporations, it seems to me is absolutely wrong in principle and in practice. We are told that the corporations need these men. If they do they should employ them for the year round and pay them substantial salaries.
I must protest against this whole practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
My hon. friend is making a mountain out of'a mole hill. The practice is in the interest of the mining industry of Canada, although I admit that it should be exercised with due caution.
I understand that it is the practice of all geological surveys to do the very thing we are doing. Many years ago Dr. Barlow went to Sudbury and made a scientific survey of the nickel deposits in the interest of the nickel industry there, and his work is said to have resulted in very great benefit to the country. The department

lost nothing whatever by that; nor did it lose anything by permitting one of the geologists, who is an expert in coal, to go into the country west of Edmonton and assist in the exploration of an area of land in the mountains known to contaon coal, and known long ago to contain coal. He did not lead the company to the coal field or give them any information as to the location of the coal deposits. We have known for many years that the coal existed in that northern country.
Should not that information be kept for the benefit of the people and not used to enable private individuals to make money?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is published in the report of the Geological Survey.
Then why did these people want the man?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Because they needed his services and paid for them. If we had not allowed him to go, he would have been in the employ of that company to-day, and we would have lost his services; there is the whole question. Until two years ago Dr. Barlow was in the service of the Geological Survey at a salary of between $2,000 and $3,000; he was one of the best-men in the service, and was offered $5,000 a year by a German company operating in the west and having large investments in Canada, and he is with that company today and we have lost his services. Mr. McEvoy, who was a long time in the Survey, and was one of our best men, was until recently in the employ of the Crow's Nest Coal Company, receiving three times the salary we paid him.

Is the minister aware that Mr. Dowling, after making his report, spent five years in this district with a number of employees, all of whom were paid by the government, and that he did not make his final report on these locations until last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend is not well informed. It is true Mr. Dowling worked in that part of the country for many years. He always returned to Ottawa in the fall, wrote his report, and it was published. The country at large has all the information collected by Mr. Dowling and has had it for years, so that any person could have gone to that country and staked out a coal location. If my hon. friend wants to stake out a coal location, he can do so, as there is plenty in British Columbia ; the whole country is full of coal. I think the practice is in the interest of the mining industry.

If Mr. Dowling made a Teport in regard to these mines, why was it not made in connection with these companies? Other companies who Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
are anxious to operate in that country send out men themselves to locate the mines, but Mr. Dowling, having been there for years, knew exactly where he could go and locate them, which he did. I do not think it is fair to the people of the country generally to say that anybody is allowed to go and locate mines.
In what year was Mr. Dowling in this district?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: When was his report published?

provide also for his salary next year. Professor Prince was receiving the salary of $2,500, and it is proposed to give him $4,000 and to put him in the first division, subdivision ' A.' The minister gave us to understand the other day that such regulations as Professor Prince would make as an international commissioner would be laid before the department and parliament and would be liable to be changed by parliament. I think the minister was in error, and I want to call his attention to the fact that the treaty states that the finding of the commissioners is final and that the department and parliament has nothing to do with it.
Except that there is a provision in the treaty to this effect:

The two governments engage to put into operation and to enforce by legislation and executive action, with as little delay as possible, the regulations, restrictions, and provisions with appropriate penalties for all breaches thereof.
So that when the regulations have been adopted by the two commissioners they are to be laid before the government and the government has to come before parliament for the purpose of securing the necessary legislation to enforce the regulations.

But parliament would be obliged to pass them. They could not change the regulations or reprimand Professor Prince if he had done wrongly. Therefore, the minister will see that my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) is quite right in saying that parliament has no control over the matter. The treaty is that the two governments engage to enforce by legislation what these two commissioners do.
We will have to come to parliament for the purpose of having legislation passed to enforce these regulations.
You bind yourself to adopt them.

Of course, the government would have to take the responsibility

of these regulations and if they are not proper regulations the government would be liable to censure.

That does not appear to be the feature of it at all. We understood that whatever these regulations were parliament had to concur in them or otherwise they could not become law. Now, we find that we have to pass legislation affirming them but that does not mean that we can change them.
Parliament would have to pass legislation to enforce these regulations, and if they did not meet with the approval of the House parliament would have the right to refuse the necessary sanction.
No; the treaty says distinctly that the two parties bind themselves to carry into effect the regulations which may be made by these two commissioners.
Suppose the government were not able to secure the passage of this legislation ?

The argument could be made that you would be liable to get into a war with this other country for breaking the treaty if you failed to carry it out. Surely the British government, when it makes that treaty, expects to carry it out and engages to enforce the regulations that the two commissioners make in so far as they can be enforced by legislation. The hon. gentleman pre-supposes that parliament might not concur in them, but parliament would have to swallow them or else throw the British government into the most deplorable position of having broken a treaty made with another country and which might be a cause for war.

It is the same with all treaties made by Great Britain. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that treaties made by Great Britain are not submitted to or approved by parliament except in cases where an expenditure of money is involved. I think also there is an exception in the case of commercial treaties which require some amendment to the Customs Act. These are the only cases provided for by the constitution in which treaties are referred to parliament. In other cases a treaty, as passed by the Crown, becomes the law of the land.
Did not the French and Japanese treaties require the ratification of this parliament ?

Yes, because it was formally provided in these two treaties that they had to be approved by parliament. These two treaties fell within the category of the treaties which I have just mentioned; that is to say, they were treaties requiring a change in customs law. There is a principle in the British constitution to the
effect that taxation cannot be imposed even by the King without the sanction of parliament. The King would have no right to make any treaty by which taxation would be levied or expenditure incurred without the consent of the parliament of Great Britain. Such a treaty affecting Canada would require to be submitted to the Canadian parliament by the representative of the King here. But, those treaties which are signed by the King or his representative have not to be approved by parliament, and this is a treaty made by the King with the president of the United States.

It is an old established principle of international law that where there is constitutional government when a treaty is made affecting territory or property or money, that treaty must be laid before parliament.
Not in the case of territory, I think.
Yes; if you have read the discussion on the Napoleonic Code you will know that.

Under the British constitution a treaty made by the King is law without being submitted for the approbation of parliament. There are only two cases where such treaties have to be ratified by parliament. First, where they may levy taxation on the country and, second, where they may cause expenditure.

Then these reasons apply in the ease of this treaty, because those two commissioners are given power with regard to our fisheries that may result in more concern to the country than if they affected either territory or taxation. Upon the minister's own statement this parliament would be bound to ratify the regulations laid down by these two commissioners under that teraty. There is no use trying to hypnotize ourselves into any other belief, for we would have no power to change these regulations without putting Great Britain on the verge of war.
It is the same with any treaty which the King makes.

If it is the same it is time Canada should raise her voice to stop it. I am not here to dictate what Great Britain should do, but if Great Britain says that we must approve of any regulations which these two men may make it seems to me it is practically unconstitutional. This country elects 220 members of narliament to deal with her affairs, and we should not be asked to leave it in the power of two men to dispose of our great assets in the fisheries for four years. If Great Britain has not said that these regulations shall be subject to the approval of the Canadian parliament, Great Britain ought

to have said it. Such a proceeding renders this parliament helpless and pledges us ahead of time to do what these commissioners may decide or else to place Great Britain in the position of breaking her contract with the United States. I am still of the opinion that we have no power whatever over these regulations once they are made.
It has been one of the boasts of this government and of the Minister of Marine in particular that a new era had arrived and that Canada herself had now all to do with the making of treaties.
Commercial treaties.

But now the minister announces that these treaties are made by England and that we have nothing at all to say about them. How can he justify that statement with his declarations to the contrary all over the country?
Formerly commercial treaties were made without the concurrence of the Canadian parliament or the consent of the Canadian government.
Are they yet?

There are many commercial treaties affecting Canada which have never been submitted to the Canadian parliament or to the Canadian government. In the case of Switzerland, a treaty is declared to include Canada, although Canada has absolutely nothing to do with the negotiation of that treaty in 1885. Later on when commercial treaties were being negotiated Great Britain began at first by giving us a plenipotentiary on the -commission, and then she gave us the advantage of negotiating them absolutely ourselves. In some cases where negotiations had been carried out entirely by Great Britain there was a clause in the treaty providing that it would not affect Canada without her consent.
Which class does this one belong to?

This belongs to the class which is known as political treaties. I am afraid there may be some misapprehension with regard to this matter and so I may be permitted to explain. Mind you, we are living under the principles of the British constitution, and in Great Britain all treaties made by the King-with the exception of commercial treaties by which taxation may be levied or expense incurred -become law without the sanction of the British parliament.
Would the King consent to give away colonial territory without the consent of the parliament of the colony?

I do not know whether that would be done without submitting the Mr. LANCASTER.
luestion to the Canadian government, and I make a distinction between the Canadian government and the Canadian parliament. The point of the hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) is that all these treaties should be submitted to the Canadian parliament before they are ratified, but I think he is going too far in that. I think we should be very well pleased that no treaty should be made affecting Canada without the consent of the Canadian government.
Mr, LANCASTER. Is this treaty one of
these?
Yes.
