Certainly.
Then the Canadian government is to blame.

Yes, if there is anything wrong in that treaty we arei responsible for it just the same as the British government would be responsible for any similar treaties made in Great Britain. They are signed in the name of the King, and the British government is responsible for them. In the same way we assume the responsibility of this treaty. I do not know whether we get by it everything we asked, but I think we get almost everything. What my hon. friend suggests is that all treaties affecting Canada should be submitted to the Canadian parliament for its approval. Treaties made by the British government are not submitted to the British parliament for its approval, and can we ask the King to do for the Canadian parliament what he is not doing for the British parliament?
If conditions exist which make it reasonable, why should we not?
That has been the rule of the British constitution for centuries, and before we can get that changed for Canada, I suppose the British parliament will ask that it be changed for Great Britain.	i	,

The British government has changed its habits with respect to consulting Canada with regard to treaties affecting this country. It is said that it will not make such treaties without the consent of the Canadian government. I do not see why it would not be proper to ask the British government to make such treaties subject to the approval of the parliament of Canada, to which that government is responsible.

We are taking the constitution as it is. We have made a step

in the right direction, I think, because formerly these treaties were made without being submitted to the Canadian government. In England no treaty is made without the consent and concurrence of the British government, not the British parliament. The British parliament never interferes in the making of treaties except in cases where there is a question of taxation or expenditure. In no other case has the British parliament ever been called upon to approve of a treaty, though it might pass a vote of censure on the government for having agreed to it. The constitution is precisely the same in Canada. We are now in this position, that no treaty affecting Canada will be made without being submitted to the approval of the Canadian government. I think that is a step in the right direction. Perhaps changes may some time be made in England in the direction my hon. friend suggests; I would not object to that. But for the moment I suppose we must be satisfied that the parliament of Canada is treated in the same way as the parliament of Great Britain, because we are living under British institutions and under the rules of the British constitution.

Does the hon. minister say that the Canadian authorities could not have insisted on a provision in that treaty that it should be ratified by the Canadian parliament, just as the United States authorities insisted that it must obtain the ratification of the Senate of the United States? 1

I am glad my hon. friend has brought up the question of the United States constitution. There is a great deal of misapprehension in this country on that subject. In the United States there is no responsible government. The President and his ministers are not responsible to parliament. The constitution of the United States provides that a treaty may not be made by the President and his ministers alone, but must be made with the advice and consent of the United States Senate-not Congress. The house of representatives is not called on to express any view of a treaty, unless, I suppose, it related to taxation or expenditure. But the United States Senate, under the constitution, participates in the making of treaties.
And is responsible to the people.	*

Senators are not elected directly by the people, but by the local legislatures. Some people in this country have thought it extraordinary that the United States Senate had something to do with the treaty recently made, and I am
giving my hon. friend the reasons for that. We are not living under the United States constitution. I hope we shall never have a constitution like that of the United States. I do not want to make any comparisons, but I think our constitution is far superior, to theirs. We are living under British constitutional principles, and according to those principles the King has the right to make treaties without submitting them to parliament.

But if the government is responsible to the people, I cannot understand why the hon. gentleman objects to the government seeing that parliament' shall approve of their action in the important matter of making treaties. What I want to protest against is that this government has consented to this clause, which gives this one man, representing the whole of Canada, the power to tie us up, without any changes or qualifications, for four years, to anything he chooses to do with regard to the fisheries of this country. No matter how bad it may be we cannot object to it.

I do not know whether it is necessary for me to say anything about Professor Prince. I think every member of this House will agree with me that he is well able to carry out the duty imposed upon him by that treaty. He has been in the service of the department for many years, and there is no man in Canada perhaps who knows more of our fisheries. He has been connected with all the investigations into the subject made during the years that he has been in the department, and has always given satisfaction and promoted the interest of the country. I am not going to-day to discuss the merits of that treaty; I hope we may have an opportunity to do so on another occasion. I will only say that I believe it will be found to be a treaty that will be to the advantage of our Canadian fisheries.

I hope it will be to the advantage of our Canadian fisheries; but before we can discover whether it will be or not, it will be too late; the opportunity to make any protest will have gone. The discussion this afternoon has rather surprised me. I was not aware that the British government or the King would undertake to negotiate with the United States in a matter of such special interest to the people of this country, without being called on to do so by the Canadian government, or without having the subject matter of the treaty brought to their attention.
Surely the government must have taken the initiative and requested that a treaty be negotiated between Canada and the United States touching the important matter of our inland fisheries. It will be a surprise to those deeply interested in that industry to learn that their interests can be

dealt' with in this manner. I am saying nothing about the qualifications of Professor Prince. I am confident that he will do his best in our interests, but he is only one and will be obliged to give way in certain matters if regulations are to be mutually agreed upon. While I have every confidence in Professor Prince, I regret that a treaty should have been negotiated in the manner in which this has been with regard to such an important interest. I assume that this government must have submitted the (juestion to the King with the view of obtaining a treaty, and I regret that they [DOT]did not insist so that it should not go into force before getting the assent of parliament.
It has been submitted to the government.

But the people are to have no opportunity of seeing it or saying a word about it until it comes into force. This is a very far reaching treaty, embracing interest of great importance to a large section of our people, and I can only express my surprise and regret that the government should have permitted a treaty to be negotiated under such conditions.

My understanding of several replies given with regard to that treaty was very different from what we are given to understand by the minister to-day. Several times the question has been brought to the attention of the House, and on each occasion the answer given created the impression on my mind that if there was anything in the treaty not satisfactory to parliament, parliament might not concur in it and it could not become law. The minister draws a distinction between government and parliament. Well, the government is the executive of parliament, and when the hon. minister was. explaining the advantages accruing to our country from the wider rights secured by the present government, among these he put the right of Canada to concur in everything and negotiate everything affecting her interests before anything could be done. Now he says that the King makes the treaty and parliament has nothing to do with it at all. That does not leave parliament free to decide whether the treaty is good or bad.
That is the way it is done in England.
That is not what the minister this session led us to believe was the right his government has secured from the imperial parliament in the making of treaties.
Commercial treaties.

The hon. gentleman did not distinguish ? He says now that this is a political treaty and different from a commercial one. Well, it is a treaty in which Mr. HENDERSON.
we have an interest that may be represented by money. Was there not a provision in the Fisheries treaty of 1888 that it was to be submitted to parliament and approved by parliament ?
No. My hon. friend is referring to the Bayard-Chamberlain treaty. That was never approved by the United States Senate, and consequently never came into force.
Was there not a provision in the agreement that it should have the concurrence of the Canadian parliament before it became law ?

The treaty was never submitted to our parliament. I am not sure whether there was such a clause or not, but at all events it was never put before parliament here. In fact the treaty was never made because by the United States constitution a treaty must receive the approval of the United States Senate, and this never got that approval.

The treaty was made just as much as the French treaty, which was negotiated by this government within the last year or two. So far as the two governments are concerned, their representatives discussed the whole question and signed the treaty.
The Chamberlain-Bayard treaty never got the consent of the United States Senate.

Neither has the French treaty , received the assent of the French Senate. The treaty was concluded and signed by the plenipotentiaries of both countrie.s, then it went to the president of the United States and he approved it and sent it to the United States Senate, and that body smothered it.

Under the British constitution a treaty is negotiated by the King or his plenipotentiaries with the advice and consent of his government. In the United States a treaty is negotiated by the plenipotentiaries, but before it is ratified it must have the assent of the United States Senate. In fact the United States Senate, in the negotiation of treaties, takes the same position as the British government.
It is the treaty making power.

I would suggest that it would be well to let Professor Prince's duties be entirely devoted to international work. I know that the minister is very anxious to employ him, but he holds a very honourable position and I would like to make this suggestion.

Of course, it might be very becoming to have Professor Prince devote all his time to this International Com-

mission. But he has been our scientist expert for many years and the chairman of many commissions. My hon. friend knows how competent he is on these questions. We cannot spare him from the department. We have men in the department who are qualifying themselves for these duties, and some day Professor Prince may be able to devote himself exclusively to the international commission. But, at present, the department cannot, spare him.

The minister spoke of the differences between the American and the British constitution. I assume that all the members of this House were aware of the differences pointed out by the minister, but I do not think that anything the hon. gentleman said answered the suggestion I made that the British plenipotentiaries representing the British government on bd-half of the Dominion of Canada might have proposed the insertion of a clause in this treaty requiring ratification by the parliament of Canada. I am satisfied that the British ministers would not have made any objection to such a course if it had been proposed by the Canadian government. There are several reasons why it seems to me ratification by the parliament of Canada should have been made a condition of this treaty. The province of New Brunswick is interested, not only with respect to the waters that form the international boundary line, but with respect to all of the waters of the St. John river, the principal waterway of the province, which is wholly controlled so far as its fisheries are concerned, by the provisions of this treaty. Formerly, the fisheries of the St. John, as all the fisheries of the Dominion, were under the control of the people through their representatives in the parliament of Canada. Now, this treaty has been negotiated

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) will permit me:	This question has to be discussed in a few days on the motion of my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor). If it is possible I would like to have these estimates go through. The question of the St. John river is one on which there is much to be said, and on which I would like some time to answer. The matter is outside this vote

I will not take much time. I was saying that, formerly, the fisheries of the St. John river, as the fisheries of all Canada, were under the control of the parliament of Canada. We had a fisheries law, passed by the people's representatives, regulating these fisheries. This treaty, as I understand it, has absolutely taken out of the control of parliament, and placed in
the hands of a commission of two, one of whom is representative of a foreign government, the control of the waters of the St. John river, so far as fisheries are concerned,-not only where that river forms the international boundary, but down to the harbour of St. John.
And also in the United States.

I am speaking of the effect on the Dominion of Canada. It seems to me most surprising that a government which professes to represent the Dominion of Canada should have placed in the hands of a commission of this kind such immense powers and that we can have no regulation of the fisheries, not only of the St. John but of its tributaries, without the consent of an appointee of the United States government. Nothing that the minister has said this afternoon justifies this treaty as it has been negotiated, and I think that the very fact that these fisheries are taken out of the control of the parliament of Canada and these large powers which were formerly vested in this parliament placed in the hands of a commission composed as I have indicated was good reason why there should have been inserted in that treaty a provision that it should not be effective without the consent of the representatives of the people in this parliament.
Now, one word-as I may not have an opportunity when the matter comes up- on the practical effect of what has been done. I would point out to the minister that great interest is taken in this matter by the people living along the St. John river. The minister knows that we had on the statute-book a law prohibiting salmon fisheries in the non-tidal waters of the St. John, and other rivers. But, for years, that law was a dead letter; so far as the St. John river was concerned, it was not observed, and the government did not attempt to enforce it. A few years ago, the government began the enforcement of the law in the non-tidal waters of the St. John river, with the result that such a furore was raised among the people, that the government were compelled last year to put through an order in council giving the people living along the St. John the right, to fish for salmon with nets during every alternate fortnight during the open season. That concession has been done away with by the negotiation of this treaty, without reference to the wishes of the people or of their representatives, and without giving the people's representatives any chance to be heard with respect to the matter. For my part, I have not been able to see why the residents along the St. John river above Fredericton should not be entitled to the-same privileges as those below Fredericton.

In the tidal waters, the people have the right to fish for salmon during the open season. Under the order in council passed last year, the people above Fredericton were limited to fishing during every alternate fortnight. This treaty has taken the question out of our hands, and I can say to the minister that the treaty will be most unpopular among the people living along that river, and he will find that the provision divesting this parliament of such powers will raise a pretty serious issue in the province of New Brunswick. I do not think that one word the minister has said this afternoon answers the objection I have made that there might have been inserted in this treaty a provision requiring ratification by this parliament before the treaty became effective.

I will not discuss the question of the River St. John, because we will have an opportunity of dealing with it when the motion of my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) is made, and I understand that will be within a few days. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) says that this treaty does away with the present regulations. Let him wait until the regulations have been passed by the Commission, and he will find, probably, that the present regulations have not been done away with.
Does not the treaty give to the International Commission the right to make regulations?

Yes. But that does not mean that the present regulations will necessarily be done away with. The hon. gentleman says the present regulations will disappear. But nothing has been done to justify him in saying that. As to the St. John river, of course the hon. gentleman 'confines himself to that part which is in Canadian territory. But the St. John river flows through a part of the state of Maine, and over that part the Canadian commissioner will have as much to say as the American commissioner will have to say with regard to the lower part of the river. The object is to protect the fisheries in both 'countries. My hon. friend is aware that one of the serious questions in relation to the St. John river is the throwing of sawdust into the river, and that difficulty arises principally in that part of the river which is in the United States. Suppose that some regulations are made by the commissioners under which this throwing of sawdust into the river will be done away with, does not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) think that will greatly improve the situation? Does he not think it would be a great improvement upon the situation? Does he not think it would be worth while to have more investigation in such a case. I suppose he would agree with me. Well, these Mr. CROCKET.
iffairs which have been exclusively exercised by the state of Maine, are now going :o be exercised by an independent commission. That is where I see some advantage.

It is quite true, as the minister states, that this treaty gives the International Commission control of the waters of the St. John Tiver that are in the United States as well as of the waters that are in the Dominion of Canada. But I think the minister will see that that does not count for much in so far as the fisheries are concerned. The United States have practically no interest in the fisheries of the St. John river because Grand Falls is an absolute barrier to the progress of fish up the Tiver; fish do not go further up the river than Grand Falls, and Grand Falls is a good many miles from the international boundary. So in that view it seems to me a, most extraordinary thing to contemplate that a commission composed of two members, one of them an appointee of the United States government, a citizen of a foreign country, should have any voice in regulating the fisheries in all the waters of the St. John, even in the St. John harbour, and in every tributary of the St. John river. Now that the minister has admitted, as we were all well aware, that this government were responsible for negotiating this treaty, I am satisfied he will find before long that the treaty will not-have done the government very much good, at least in the province of New Brunswick.

The statement just made by my hon. friend proves that the government was justified in putting the St. John river among the boundary waters, and the regulations regarding the fisheries in that river under the control of this commission. The hon. gentleman says that the fisheries exist in that part of the river which is wholly in Canadian territory.
And the United States has no interest in them. Why should it control them?

Let us see what interest Canada has in it. Our fisheries are being depleted in the St. John river to-day by the dumping of sawdust in a part of the St. John river which is in American territory. From this cause our fisheries in Canadian territory were threatened with absolute destruction. Now when we get permission from the American authorities to appoint a commission with power to deal with this question of sawdust, I think we have done a great deal for the protection of our fisheries in the St. John river. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman should find fault with this government, when he knows that the Americans are dumping sawdust in the St. John river and its tributaries, the result of which our fisheries from the bound-

ary to the sea were likely, to be destroyed. Now, through this commission, we are going to have some jurisdiction over those waters, a jurisdiction that we had not before; therefore, instead of blaming this government for negotiating this treaty, I think this government is deserving of commendation for having included the St. John river among those over which the commission will have authority.

As to the regulation of salmon fishing in the non-tidal waters of the St. John, I understand the minister to say that there are no regulations promulgated as yet. Now if the minister has any control over this subject, I trust that he will see that the people living along the banks of the St. John in the non-tidal waters above Fredericton, will be put in the same position as those living below Fredericton. I trust that the minister will bear that representation in mind, if he has any voice in making these regulations.
Will the minister tell us what are Admiral Kingsmill's duties?
Admiral Kingsmill has charge of the fisheries protection service; he discharges the same duties as were performed by Commander Spain.
He is discharging no other duties except those that come under the ordinary routine covered by Captain Spain?
He has charge of the discipline and control of the fleet, if I may call it so; he has also to see that discipline is observed on the other boats engaged in buoying and lighting.
Is that the line of service for which the government secured Admiral Kingsmill?
We secured his services to take charge of our fisheries and protection service, and to develop the naval militia which was mentioned some time ago.
What has he done with reference to that, matter?

He has been instructed to look into the matter, and to prepare information for the government and the minister.	i [.
Mr. FOSTER Has he made any progress up to the present time?
I have not yet received any formal report.
With reference to these 78 outside and temporary employees, were these all transferred into the service on the 1st of September at the same salaries with which they began the year, that is, April 1?

They have all been transferred with the same salary, with some exceptions. Department of Marine and Fisheries-contingencies, $21,000.

No, the vote is the same as last year.
And some of the clerical force has been put on the permanent list.
There were no salaries under contingencies before; so I am informed by the acting deputy. We had a special vote for that purpose.
Who is now the deputy minister ?
There is no one. Mr. Desbarats is acting deputy.
Who is intended to be deputy minister ?
It is not decided yet.
The minister has not made up his mind ?
Not absolutely.
Now; now !
I have an open mind.
As I understand it, the old deputy is superannuated ?
Yes.

The superannuation has
actually taken place ?
No, it has not passed the Treasury Board. I understand that it has to go before the Treasury Board.
Until it passes the Treasury Board the minister has an open mind?

An open mind as to the appointment of a new one.
Some resolutions reported.

I would like to know if the hon. Minister of Agriculture intends to bring on the Civil Service resolution and Bill to be founded thereon before Easter ?

I should be very glad to do so but I doubt if there 'will be an opportunity. We cannot proceed until the classifications of the House and of the Senate have been passed. The classification of the House has been before the House for some days in the name of the Prime Minister. That as well as the Senate classification will have to be adopted.
There is not much probability of it going on ?
No I do not think so.
I suppose we might say the same as to the Finance Minister's budget speech ?
